knowledge-base.overview: Official Python naming conventions, type hint patterns, and style rules from PEP 8, PEP 484, and the Google Python Style Guide. Covers what is NOT already in lang-python.xml: specific naming rules across every identifier kind, __all__ discipline, logging module setup, docstring format, and walrus operator guidance.

naming-conventions.description: Python naming conventions from PEP 8 and the Google style guide. Every identifier kind has a specific casing rule.

rules.rule: module_name: lowercase with underscores (also used for packages). Example: `user_service`, `data_pipeline`
ClassName: CapWords (PascalCase). Example: `UserService`, `DataPipeline`
method_name and function_name: lowercase with underscores. Example: `get_user`, `process_batch`
CONSTANT_NAME: uppercase with underscores. Example: `MAX_RETRY_COUNT`, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`
_protected_name: single leading underscore for protected/internal use. Example: `_parse_token`
__private_name: double leading underscore triggers name mangling — only for true class-private attributes where subclasses must not accidentally override. Use sparingly.
__dunder__: reserved for Python's special protocol methods (str, repr, init, len, etc.). Never invent your own dunder names.
Exception classes: always suffix with Error. Example: `ValidationError`, `NotFoundError`
Avoid single-character names except for counters (i, j), type variables (T, K, V), exception handlers (e), and file handles (f)
Never use dashes in module names or package names (use underscores). Never use offensive terms. No type-encoding in names (not `user_dict` — just `users`).

all-exports.description: __all__ controls what `from module import *` exports and serves as an explicit public API contract. Define it in every public module.

rules.rule: Define `__all__` in every public module (any module intended to be imported by external code). This documents the public API and prevents accidental export of internal helpers.
List only the identifiers you intend to be part of the public interface. Private names (_name) are never included.
Internal modules (prefixed with _) may omit `__all__` since they are not part of the public API.
Keep `__all__` near the top of the file, after imports and before class/function definitions

all-exports.example:
# user_service.py from __future__ import annotations
from .models import User from .repository import UserRepository
__all__ = ["UserService", "UserServiceError"] # explicit public API
class UserServiceError(Exception): pass
class UserService: def __init__(self, repo: UserRepository) -> None: self._repo = repo
def _build_cache_key(user_id: str) -> str: # not in __all__, internal return f"user:{user_id}"

type-hints.description: Type hint rules beyond "use them everywhere" — these are the patterns from PEP 484 and PEP 526 that appear most in practice.

rules.rule: Add `from __future__ import annotations` at the top of any file that uses forward references (types referenced before they are defined). This defers annotation evaluation and avoids NameError.
Prefer `X | None` over `Optional[X]` (Python 3.10+). Prefer `X | Y` over `Union[X, Y]`. The `|` syntax is more readable and aligns with modern Python.
Use `collections.abc` types for generics in annotations: `Sequence`, `Mapping`, `Iterable`, `Callable`. Never use `typing.List`, `typing.Dict`, `typing.Tuple` — those are deprecated aliases.
Import type symbols directly: `from typing import Any, TypeVar` not `import typing; typing.Any`
Use TypeVar for generic functions. Constrain with bound= when you need to access specific attributes.
For classmethods that return an instance of the class, use `Self` from `typing` (Python 3.11+) rather than a string forward reference.
Annotate `__init__` parameters but omit the return type annotation (it is always `None`). Omit `self` and `cls` annotations.

logging.description: Python logging setup. The lang-python.xml guardrails cover error handling broadly; these rules cover the logging module specifically.

rules.rule: Create a module-level logger with `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. This gives each module its own logger namespace and lets the application control log levels per module.
Never use print() for diagnostic output or application logging. Use the logging module so output can be controlled, filtered, and routed by the application's logging configuration.

Pass arguments to logging methods as positional args, NOT with f-strings: `logger.info("User %s created", user_id)` not `logger.info(f"User {user_id} created")`. This preserves the unformatted message template and avoids string formatting cost when the log level is disabled.

Log at the right level: DEBUG for detailed flow, INFO for significant events, WARNING for unexpected but recoverable, ERROR for failures that need attention, CRITICAL for application-breaking failures.
Log errors with exc_info=True or logger.exception() inside except blocks to include the stack trace.
Never log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII) even at DEBUG level.

comprehensions.description: When to use list/dict/set comprehensions vs loops, and where they become unreadable.

rules.rule: Prefer list/dict/set comprehensions over map() and filter() calls for simple transformations. Comprehensions are more Pythonic and readable.
Keep comprehensions to a single for-clause and at most one if-clause on a single line. If you need more, write a regular loop.
Never nest more than two comprehension levels. Nested comprehensions beyond two for-clauses are harder to read than explicit loops.

Use a generator expression (round brackets) instead of a list comprehension when the result is consumed immediately without being stored, e.g. `sum(x * x for x in items)` instead of `sum([x * x for x in items])`

comprehensions.example:
# Good: simple comprehension active_users = [u for u in users if u.is_active] name_map = {u.id: u.name for u in users}
# Good: generator for immediate consumption total = sum(order.total for order in orders)
# WRONG: nested comprehension beyond two levels matrix = [[cell for cell in row if cell > 0] for row in grid if sum(row) > 0]
# RIGHT: explicit loop when comprehension gets complex result = [] for row in grid: if sum(row) > 0: for cell in row: if cell > 0: result.append(cell)
# Comprehension over map/filter # WRONG: names = list(map(lambda u: u.name, filter(lambda u: u.is_active, users))) # RIGHT: names = [u.name for u in users if u.is_active]

walrus-operator.description: The walrus operator (:=) assigns a value within an expression. Use it sparingly.

rules.rule: Use the walrus operator only when it eliminates genuine duplication in an expression and makes the code clearer, not shorter-for-its-own-sake.
Appropriate uses: while-loop that reads and processes, comprehension with an expensive expression that you filter and use, conditional expressions that call the same function twice.
Never use walrus just to save a line. If a regular assignment on the line before is clearer, use that.

walrus-operator.example:
# Good: walrus in while loop eliminates repetition while chunk := file.read(8192): process(chunk)
# Good: comprehension with expensive call used twice results = [y for x in data if (y := expensive_transform(x)) is not None]
# WRONG: walrus where a plain assignment is clearer if (n := len(items)) > 10: # just write: n = len(items); if n > 10: print(f"Too many items: {n}")

docstrings.description: Docstring format following Google Python Style Guide (triple double-quotes, structured sections).

rules.rule: Use triple double-quotes for all docstrings: `"""Summary."""`
One-line docstrings: a single sentence summary ending with a period, on one line including the quotes
Multi-line docstrings: one-line summary, blank line, then body. Use structured sections: Args:, Returns: (or Yields:), Raises:
Public functions, methods, classes, and modules require docstrings. Private helpers and trivial functions may omit them.
Document the meaning of parameters, not just their names. Mention units, ranges, or invariants where relevant.

docstrings.example:
def fetch_user(user_id: str, *, include_deleted: bool = False) -> User | None: """Fetch a user by ID from the database.
Args: user_id: The UUID of the user to fetch. include_deleted: When True, also searches soft-deleted records.
Returns: The User if found, or None if no user with that ID exists.
Raises: DatabaseError: If the database is unreachable. """ ...

imports.description: Import ordering and style from PEP 8 and Google style guide. These supplement lang-python.xml which covers star imports and relative imports.

rules.rule: Use `import x` for packages and modules. Use `from x import y` where y is a module or a well-known symbol. Never import individual classes/functions from deeply nested paths unless the path would otherwise be unreadably long.
Never use relative imports (from . import foo). Always use full package paths: `from myapp.models import User`
Group imports in order: (1) `from __future__` imports, (2) standard library, (3) third-party, (4) local package. Blank line between each group. Sort lexicographically within groups.
Import type annotations directly from typing: `from typing import Any, TypeVar` — not `import typing` and then `typing.Any`

imports.example:
from __future__ import annotations # always first if present
import logging # stdlib import os from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import Any
import httpx # third-party from pydantic import BaseModel
from myapp.config import Settings # local from myapp.models import User

quick-reference.item: CapWords. Exception classes end in Error.
Define in every public module. Lists the public API.
X | None not Optional[X]. X | Y not Union[X, Y].
Add annotations import when using forward references.
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__). Never print(). Pass args not f-strings.
One for-clause + one if max. Never nested beyond two levels. Prefer over map/filter.
Use only when it genuinely removes duplication. Never just to save a line.
Triple double-quotes. Args/Returns/Raises sections. Period at end of summary.
No relative imports. Group: future / stdlib / third-party / local. Direct from typing imports.
